name: Legends of the Pacific — Maui, Hina & the Great Voyagers
description: Eleven chapters: nine traditional stories of Polynesia — Maui the trickster, Hina, Pele, Rata, and Kupe — retold in original words for young readers and read-aloud nights. These are the real legends beneath the movies: told across the Pacific for more than a thousand years, older than any studio. Each chapter ends with a Wonder Together question and a note for the grown-up.

attribution.source_author: Traditional — as recorded in W. D. Westervelt, 'Legends of Ma-ui — a Demi God of Polynesia and of his Mother Hina' (Honolulu, 1910) and other public-domain collections
attribution.license: Traditional stories are not owned by anyone. These retellings are original text, CC-BY-SA-4.0, by PlayfulProcess.
attribution.note: Retold gently for young children. Some legends exist in many island versions (Hawaiian, Maori, Samoan, Tahitian, Fijian); each retelling notes its main thread in the For the Grown-up section. No text, characters, or lyrics from any film are used.

items.name: How Maui Fished Up the Islands

sections.Story:
Long, long ago, Maui was the youngest brother, and his brothers never let him come fishing. So one night he hid in the bottom of their canoe. When they were far out at sea, he popped up! Too far to turn back now.

Maui took out a magic fishhook made from his grandmother's jawbone. He dipped it deep, deep, deep — and something ENORMOUS pulled back.

He pulled and chanted. His brothers paddled and groaned. The sea boiled white around them. And up from the bottom of the ocean came... land! A whole island, huge as a fish, dripping with seaweed, flapping with rivers, shining in the sun.

Some say the islands of the Pacific are all fish that Maui pulled up from the deep. When you stand on an island, you are standing on Maui's catch.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
If you could fish up your own island, what would be on it?
sections.Wonder Together: If you could fish up your own island, what would be on it?
sections.For the Grown-up: One of the most widespread Maui stories in all of Polynesia. In Aotearoa (New Zealand), the North Island is called Te Ika-a-Maui — 'the fish of Maui' — and the South Island is his canoe.

metadata.chapter_name: How Maui Fished Up the Islands

sections.Story:
In the old days, the Sun raced across the sky as fast as he pleased. Days were so short that people could not fish, could not plant, could not dry their clothes. Night came before anyone was ready.

Maui said: ENOUGH.

He and his brothers wove strong ropes from flax. They traveled east, all the way to the pit where the Sun sleeps, and laid their ropes like a net around it. When the Sun rose up, roaring and blazing — they PULLED. The ropes held!

The Sun thrashed and burned, but Maui would not let go. Not until the Sun made a promise: I will walk slowly across the sky.

And that is why days are long enough to fish, to plant, to play — and to watch the sunset all the way to the end.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
What would you do with one extra-long day?
sections.Wonder Together: What would you do with one extra-long day?
sections.For the Grown-up: A story about bargaining with forces bigger than you — not destroying the Sun, just slowing it. Told from Hawaii (where it happens on Haleakala, 'House of the Sun') to Aotearoa.

items.name: How Maui Brought Fire to People

sections.Story:
Once, all the cooking fires in the world went out. The only fire left belonged to Mahuika, the fire goddess, who kept flames burning in her fingernails.

Maui volunteered to go get fire — but really, he was curious.

Mahuika kindly gave him one burning fingernail. Maui walked away... and dropped it in a stream! He came back. 'I lost it. May I have another?' Again and again, until Mahuika had one fingernail left and knew she had been tricked.

FURIOUS, she threw her last fire after him, and the whole world began to burn! Maui called the rain, and the rain came pouring down to save him. And Mahuika threw her very last sparks into the trees, to keep them safe from the water.

That is why, when people rub two dry sticks together, fire comes OUT of the wood. The fire has been hiding in the trees ever since.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
Maui's trick almost burned the whole world. Was getting fire worth it?
sections.Wonder Together: Maui's trick almost burned the whole world. Was getting fire worth it?
sections.For the Grown-up: A classic trickster tale: curiosity and mischief tangled together, with a real gift at the end. Good for talking about how the same person can cause the problem AND the solution.

items.name: Why Maui Wanted to Live Forever

sections.Story:
Maui had done almost everything. Slowed the sun. Fished up islands. Brought fire to people.

But people still grew old, and that seemed to Maui like the one thing left to fix. He wanted to defeat death itself, so that no one would ever have to say goodbye.

The old stories say he went to face the great goddess of the night, Hine-nui-te-po, to try to win endless life for everyone.

He did not win. Even Maui, the greatest trickster, could not trick death.

But listen: people have told his stories for a thousand years and more. Tonight, right here, we are telling them again.

Maybe that was the way he got to live forever after all.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
Maui lives on in stories. What story about YOU should people tell in a thousand years?
sections.Wonder Together: Maui lives on in stories. What story about YOU should people tell in a thousand years?
sections.For the Grown-up: The full version of this Maori legend involves Maui's death and is usually told to older children — this retelling keeps the meaning (stories as immortality) without the frightening details.

items.name: Hina and the Eel: Why Coconuts Have Faces

sections.Story:
Hina lived by a clear pool, and in the pool lived a little eel. She fed him and he grew — and grew — and GREW — until he was Tuna, the great eel king, too big for the pool and too wild to be anyone's pet.

Tuna loved Hina, but he was frightening now. He followed her everywhere. Over the mountains her father raised. Over the new mountains her mother raised. Hina ran from village to village, and no one was brave enough to help.

At last one chief stood up for her, and Tuna's long chase came to its end. As the great eel lay dying, he called for Hina, and his voice was gentle, like the little eel in the pool.

'Bury my head beside your home,' he said. 'And you will see.'

Hina did. And out of the ground grew a tree no one had ever seen before — tall, with feathery leaves, and a fruit like a smooth brown head with two dark eyes.

The coconut. Sweet water inside, so the eel could give Hina a cool drink forever. Look at the next coconut you meet: it still has a face, still watching over her.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
The scary eel became a gift. Can you think of something scary that turned out to be something else?
sections.Wonder Together: The scary eel became a gift. Can you think of something scary that turned out to be something else?
sections.For the Grown-up: Told across Samoa (as Sina and Tuna), Tonga, Fiji, and Hawaii — one of the great origin stories of the Pacific's most important tree. Westervelt's 1910 collection records the Samoan thread. A tender one for talking about how love, fear, and loss can live in the same story.

items.name: Rata and the Canoe the Forest Built

sections.Story:
Rata needed a canoe — a great one, for a great voyage. He walked into the forest, found the tallest tree, and CHOPPED it down. He worked all day and went home proud.

In the morning, the tree was standing up again. Alive. Not even a scratch.

Rata chopped it down again. Next morning: standing again!

So the third night, Rata hid behind a fern and watched. Out came the children of the forest — the birds, the insects, the small crawling things — thousands of them, singing softly, lifting every chip and shaving back into place, healing the tree whole.

Rata stepped out. 'That is MY tree!'

The forest went silent. Then a small voice said: 'Rata. You never asked.'

Rata's face went hot. It was true. He had not asked the forest. He had not asked anyone. He bowed his head and said he was sorry.

And then — the forest children built the canoe FOR him. In one night. The finest canoe ever seen, light as a leaf, strong as the mountain. Because now it was not taken. It was given.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
What is the difference between taking something and being given it?
sections.Wonder Together: What is the difference between taking something and being given it?
sections.For the Grown-up: A beloved Maori and wider Polynesian legend about respect before use — ask the forest first. Canoe-building was sacred work, and this story carried the rule. Pairs beautifully with any conversation about asking permission.

sections.Story:
In the old homeland of Hawaiki, a giant octopus kept stealing the bait from the fishermen's hooks. Every day: lines up, bait gone. It was the pet of a jealous rival, and it was ruining everything.

Kupe said: I will follow that octopus to the end of the ocean.

He loaded the great canoe Matawhaorua with food and water. His whole family came. And the octopus swam, and Kupe followed — for days, for weeks, farther than anyone had ever sailed. At night he steered by the stars. By day he read the waves, the wind, the seabirds, the color of the water.

Then one morning Kupe's wife stood up in the canoe and shouted: 'He ao! He ao!' — A cloud! A cloud!

A long white cloud, resting on the horizon. And under a cloud like that, there is always land.

A new land no one had ever seen: Aotearoa, the land of the long white cloud. Kupe caught the octopus at last in the wild strait between the islands. And then he did the most important thing of all: he sailed home and told everyone THE WAY — the stars, the winds, the signs — so that others could follow.

The ocean is not what separates the islands. The ocean is the road.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
Kupe's wife saw the cloud first. What do you notice that grown-ups miss?
sections.Wonder Together: Kupe's wife saw the cloud first. What do you notice that grown-ups miss?
sections.For the Grown-up: Kupe is the legendary discoverer of Aotearoa in Maori tradition; his wife Kuramarotini is credited in many tellings with naming it. Real Polynesian navigation — stars, swells, birds — is one of humanity's great achievements, and 'the ocean is the road' is its heart.

sections.Story:
Hina made the most beautiful cloth in the world. She beat the bark of the mulberry tree — tap, tap, tap — until it was soft as clouds, and painted it with patterns like waves and stars.

Everyone wanted Hina's cloth. So Hina worked. And worked. And WORKED. Tap, tap, tap, from sunrise to sunset, and still they asked for more, and no one ever asked what HINA wanted.

One evening she put down her mallet and looked up.

First she tried the rainbow to the sun — but the sun's house was far too hot. So she waited for night, and climbed the rainbow's gentler curve, up and up, all the way to the moon.

And the moon was cool, and quiet, and had room for her.

She lives there still. On bright nights you can see her — Hina in the moon, with her mallet and her board. And when the sky fills with soft white clouds? That is Hina's cloth, spread out to dry.

She still makes beautiful things. But now she makes them because she wants to.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
Where is your quiet place, when you need one?
sections.Wonder Together: Where is your quiet place, when you need one?
sections.For the Grown-up: 'Hina, the Woman in the Moon' closes Westervelt's 1910 collection. A rare old story about rest — about a maker who chooses herself. Lovely last-story-before-sleep energy: she is up there right now, and the clouds are her kapa cloth.

sections.Story:
Pele carries fire inside her. Real fire — the kind that melts stone.

She crossed the ocean in a canoe, looking for a home for her fire, carrying her digging stick. On each island she dug a fire pit — but her sister, the sea, followed her everywhere, and poured into every pit, sssssss, and put it out.

Sisters can be like that.

So Pele moved on. Island after island, down the long chain, digging deeper each time, until at last she came to the great mountain Kilauea, and dug a pit so deep and so high that the sea could not reach it.

There her fire still burns.

When Pele is angry, the mountain rumbles and glowing rock pours down to the sea. People are careful and respectful, because her temper is real.

But watch what happens where the fire touches the water. The lava cools. It hardens. It becomes... NEW LAND. Black new rock where nothing was, then one green shoot, then a forest, then a shore where children play.

The one who burns is the one who builds the islands. That is the secret about Pele: her fire and her making are the same fire.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
Can a big feeling — even anger — help build something?
sections.Wonder Together: Can a big feeling — even anger — help build something?
sections.For the Grown-up: Pele is the Hawaiian volcano goddess, deeply revered in living Hawaiian culture — this story is told with respect, not as a cartoon villain. The 'destroyer who is also the creator' is the exact mythic shape kids will recognize at the end of a certain movie about the ocean.

sections.Story:
The navigators of the great ocean went to school for years — but their school had no walls, no books, and no pencils.

They memorized the star paths: which star rises from which island, and which star to follow home. But the deepest lesson was not in the sky.

It was in the body.

On long voyages, when clouds hid every star, the chief navigator would lie down in the bottom of the canoe and close her eyes. And FEEL. Every island sends its own waves across the sea, the way a dropped stone sends rings across a pond. The canoe rocks one way on open ocean, and another way when land is near. The navigator's body had learned every push and lift — the way your body knows your own bed, even in the dark.

The sailors would whisper: how can she find the way with her eyes CLOSED?

Because the stars are only half the map. The other half is written in the body.

TRY IT TONIGHT: Close your eyes. Think of something you love with your whole heart. Where do you feel it — your chest? Your belly? Your hands? Now think of something that feels wrong for you. Where does your body say no?

That feeling is your canoe. The wayfinders trusted it across two thousand miles of open water. You can trust it too.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
When your body says YES very loudly — what is it usually about?
sections.Wonder Together: When your body says YES very loudly — what is it usually about?
sections.For the Grown-up: Real technique, not metaphor: Pacific navigators steered partly by swell patterns felt through the hull — some famously navigated lying down, reading the sea with their bodies. The art was nearly lost, then revived when Mau Piailug of Satawal navigated Hokule'a from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 without instruments. This is the somatics chapter: the call Moana feels is felt in the body before it has words. And it opens the discernment conversation — inherited voices come in two kinds, the kind that protects (a sung barrier, a grandmother's call) and the kind that shames. The skill is not 'always obey the past' or 'always ignore it.' It is listening, in the body, and telling the difference.

sections.Story:
People will tell you a princess is a crown, a castle, a beautiful dress, and someone coming to the rescue.

The old stories know better.

'Princess' and 'principle' are cousin words — both grew from an ancient word meaning FIRST. Not first to be served. First to GO. First into the wave. First to keep a promise when keeping it is hard. First to say sorry. First to stand up for the smallest one.

That is the real test. Not the dress. Anyone, in any clothes, can pass it.

And here is a second secret, about heroes.

There are two ways to love a hero. You can love a hero like a LANTERN: you look at their light, and then you walk your own path, seeing better. Or you can love a hero by handing over your paddle: they steer, you ride, and slowly you forget you ever had a canoe of your own.

Here is how to tell which one you are doing. After you think about your hero — do you paddle MORE, or LESS?

A lantern-hero makes you braver in YOUR story. Keep those, and keep them bright.

But if anyone ever asks you to stop steering — even someone wonderful, even someone shiny — you may keep your paddle.

It is yours.

* WONDER TOGETHER *
Who is a lantern for you? And what are YOUR three principles — the things you would go first for?
sections.Wonder Together: Who is a lantern for you? And what are YOUR three principles — the things you would go first for?
sections.For the Grown-up: The archetype under the tiara: one who carries the principles of her people — aspiration, not decoration. Held as aspiration (the way one keeps a picture of St. Francis), an ideal enlarges you. Installed as an identity, or handed your agency, it becomes an idol — the Saja Boys in KPop Demon Hunters literalize this: idols whose adoring fans hand over their souls. Moana's refusal of the word 'princess' is the healthy half of the archetype: declining the ready-made role while quietly passing the real test. Etymology checks out, by the way: princess (princeps, 'the one who goes first') and principle (principium, 'the foundation, the first part') genuinely share a root.
